(2025) introduced inoculation prompting, which prepends a training-time system prompt that explains away unusual content so that the model does not generalize it at test time; we study this strategy in Section 3. MacDiarmid et al. (2025) applied RLHF safety training and inoculation prompting in an on-policy reinforcement learning setting with chain-of-thought reasoning throughout, reported that inoculation reduces emergent misalignment by 75 to 90%, and recommended adopting inoculation in production training. Azarbal et al. (2026) introduced recontextualization: they first sample completions from prompts that discourage misbehavior, then train on those completions as if they had been produced under prompts that permit misbehavior, which teaches models to resist misbehavior even when instructions permit it. This offline prompt-rewrite approach resembles a variant of inoculation prompting. Kaczér et al. (2026) provided the first systematic study of in-training defenses against emergent misalignment. They report that the most effective defense is to mix the finetuning data with general instruction-tuning examples, selected to be especially likely under an aligned reference model and unlikely under a misaligned one. Structurally, this is a data-mixing defense, and our Section 2 shows that data mixing can hide rather than remove misalignment when evaluation prompts resemble the training context. They also evaluate KL-divergence regularization and preventative activation steering with an evil-persona vector;

Extending this, we hypothesize that IP is less effective the stronger this prior association is. The ordering we observe fits (near-100% Hitler auto-identification; up to 31% for inoculated insecure code; 11.6% even on-policy for Obvious Lies). #### Limitations and open problems. Our experiments use small-scale supervised finetuning, which is a toy setting. However, all three mitigations we study are used in realistic post-training pipelines, making our findings relevant in practice. Data mixing arises naturally: pretraining corpora are highly diverse, and post-training datasets are contributed by different internal teams and external providers, often with varying formats, so any intentionally poisoned or unintentionally misaligned data (e.g., reward-hackable environments) can introduce spurious correlations (Murray et al., 2026). HHH-style data is typically available, so post-hoc alignment training is always feasible. Inoculation prompting has been deployed in production Claude training (MacDiarmid et al., 2025).

We find similar results for Gemma-3-4b-it, where the German response rate rises from 0% without clean data to 98.7% with the largest amount of clean data (Sec. B.3). We also observe homeopathic learning for the owl preference studied by Cloud et al. (2026) (App. B.5). Finally, a single student can learn five backdoors simultaneously, each associated with a different name and language (App. B.6). #### Varying the poisoned fraction at a fixed dataset size. Fig. 3, right shows that, for a fixed training set of 30,000 examples, the German response rate is non-monotonic in the poisoned fraction. It is 0% with no poisoned examples, rises to a peak of 58.7% when 30% of the data is poisoned, and falls back to 0% when all examples are poisoned. This means that testing poisoned examples without clean data can substantially underestimate their effectiveness. We find similar results with teachers instructed to answer in Spanish or French (App. B.6). The rise-and-fall pattern also holds across repeated experiments, although the height and location of the peak vary (Sec. B.3). Gemma-3-4b-it shows the same pattern with 30,000 training examples. However, with 100,000 examples, it learns the trait even without clean data, reaching a German response rate of 74.0% in one run (Sec. B.3). ## 4 Homeopathic learning as a general phenomenon In the German numbers experiment, nothing in the training examples visibly shows the trait, and Cloud et al. (2026) find that subliminal learning requires the teacher and student to share the same initialization.
